topics.h: Queen Ratnamanjuri's palace has 100 closed lockers and 100 visitors. Visitor 1 flips every locker, visitor 2 flips every 2nd locker, visitor 3 every 3rd... Which lockers are open at the end?
p: Visitor k flips lockers k, 2k, 3k, ... So visitor d touches locker n exactly when d is a factor of n.
A locker is flipped once for every factor it has. An odd number of flips leaves it open; an even number leaves it closed.
Factors come in pairs: 12 = 1 × 12 = 2 × 6 = 3 × 4. Only a perfect square has a pair made of one number twice (36 = 6 × 6), so only squares have an odd number of factors.
So the open lockers are the perfect squares 1, 4, 9, 16, ..., 100: ten lockers in all.
A prime number has exactly two factors (1 and itself), so a prime-numbered locker is flipped exactly twice: opened, then shut again.

ex.q: Who flips locker 12, and is it open or closed at the end?
st: That is 6 flips, an even number
Open, closed, open, closed, open, closed
ex.a: Visitors 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 flip it; it ends closed

topics.rl: Light switches work the same way: if the switch is pressed an even number of times, the lamp ends where it started.

topics.h: A school has 100 lockers and 100 students. Student 1 opens every locker, student 2 flips every 2nd locker, student 3 flips every 3rd... At the end only a few lockers are open. Which ones? The square numbers!
p: A square number is a whole number multiplied by itself: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, ... We write 7 × 7 as 7² and read it as '7 squared'.
A square number can only end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. So a number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 is never a perfect square.
Adding odd numbers from 1 builds squares: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 = 4². The sum of the first n odd numbers is n².
Between n² and (n + 1)² there are exactly 2n numbers that are not squares.
Factors come in pairs (2 × 18 = 36). In a square number one pair is a number with itself (6 × 6), so a square number has an odd count of factors. That is why only square-numbered lockers stay open!

ex.q: How many non-square numbers lie between 9² and 10²?

topics.rl: A chessboard has 8 × 8 = 64 small squares. Square floor tiles, rangoli dot grids and seating in a square hall all use square numbers.

topics.t: Squares: table, last digits, zeros and parity
topics.h: Can you tell that 3,48,723 is NOT a perfect square in one second, without any calculator? The last digit gives it away!
p: The units digit of a square depends only on the units digit of the number: 1 or 9 → 1; 2 or 8 → 4; 3 or 7 → 9; 4 or 6 → 6; 5 → 5; 0 → 0.
So a square ends only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. A number ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8 is never a square — but ending in 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9 does not prove it is one (26 is not a square).
If a number ends in k zeros, its square ends in 2k zeros. So a perfect square always ends in an even number of zeros.
Even × even is even and odd × odd is odd, so the square of an even number is even and the square of an odd number is odd.

ex.q: What is the units digit of 287²?

topics.rl: Shopkeepers and cashiers use last-digit checks to spot calculation slips quickly — the same idea works for squares.

topics.h: If you know 125² = 15625, can you find 126² in your head? A neat pattern says yes!
p: Neighbouring squares differ by an odd number: (n + 1)² − n² = n + (n + 1) = 2n + 1. For example, 13² − 12² = 12 + 13 = 25.
So the next square = this square + this number + next number: 126² = 125² + 125 + 126 = 15625 + 251 = 15876.
Triangular numbers are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, ... Two neighbouring triangular numbers always add up to a square: 6 + 10 = 16, 10 + 15 = 25.
A lovely square-sum pattern: 1² + 2² + 2² = 3², 2² + 3² + 6² = 7², 3² + 4² + 12² = 13², 4² + 5² + 20² = 21². The third number is the product of the first two, and the answer is one more than it.
Square Pairs puzzle: line up numbers so every pair of neighbours adds to a square, e.g. 8, 1, 3, 6, 10 (9, 4, 9, 16).

ex.q: Find 51² using 50² = 2500.

topics.rl: Mental-maths champions use these tricks to square numbers near 50 or 100 faster than a calculator.

topics.h: Arjun's square garden has an area of 196 m². How long is each side? Finding a square root is like running the squaring machine backwards!
p: The square root is the opposite of squaring: √81 = 9 because 9² = 81.
Prime factor method: write the number as primes, make pairs of equal primes, and take one prime from each pair. 324 = (2 × 2) × (3 × 3) × (3 × 3), so √324 = 2 × 3 × 3 = 18.
Subtraction trick: keep subtracting 1, 3, 5, 7, ... If you reach 0 after n steps, the number is n².
If a prime has no partner, multiply (or divide) by it to get a perfect square.
Estimating: √50 is between 7 and 8 because 49 < 50 < 64, and it is closer to 7.

topics.h: Aribam and Bijou play a game: one says a number, the other must reply with its square root. Bijou says 4489. Can Aribam answer without a calculator? And what if Aribam says 250, which is not a square at all?
p: A number is a perfect square exactly when every prime in its factorisation appears an even number of times (in pairs). 2025 = 3⁴ × 5² is a square; 2³ × 5² is not.
Smallest square divisible by some numbers: take their LCM, then multiply by each prime that has no partner. For 4, 9 and 10: LCM = 180 = 2² × 3² × 5, so multiply by 5 to get 900.
Square-root game, perfect squares: 4489 lies between 60² = 3600 and 70² = 4900, so the root is in the 60s. It ends in 9, so the root ends in 3 or 7. 65² = 4225 < 4489, so the root is 67.
Square-root game, non-squares: 250 is not a perfect square, but 15² = 225 < 250 < 256 = 16², and 250 is much nearer 256, so √250 is a little less than 16.
Word problems: a square of area A has side √A. To count all squares in an n × n grid, add 1² + 2² + ... + n² (a 3 × 3 grid has 9 + 4 + 1 = 14).

ex.q: Find √4489 by estimation.
st: 60² = 3600 and 70² = 4900, so the root is between 60 and 70
4489 ends in 9 → root ends in 3 or 7

topics.rl: Tile sellers use this: a square floor of 1024 square tiles needs 32 tiles along each side.

topics.t: Cubes, cube roots and the taxi number
topics.h: When the great mathematician Ramanujan was told a taxi's number, 1729, looked boring, he smiled: it is the smallest number that is a sum of two cubes in two different ways!
p: A cube number is a number multiplied by itself three times: 4³ = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. A big cube with side 4 is built from 64 small unit cubes.
Cube root is the reverse: ∛343 = 7. With prime factors, make groups of three equal primes and take one from each group.
Odd numbers make cubes too: 1 = 1³, 3 + 5 = 2³, 7 + 9 + 11 = 3³, 13 + 15 + 17 + 19 = 4³.
1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³. It is called the Hardy–Ramanujan number.

ex.q: Is 1728 a perfect cube? If yes, find ∛1728.
st: Groups of three: (2×2×2), (2×2×2), (3×3×3) — nothing left over

topics.rl: Ice cubes, dice and Rubik's cubes are cubes. A 3 × 3 × 3 Rubik's cube looks like 27 small cubes stacked together.

topics.t: Cubes of negatives, fractions and decimals; cube last digits
topics.h: Squares can never end in 2, 3, 7 or 8 — but cubes can end in ANY digit. That makes cubes even easier to spot!
p: Cubing keeps the sign: (−4)³ = −4 × −4 × −4 = −64. Fractions and decimals work too: (2/3)³ = 8/27 and (0.2)³ = 0.008.
Units digit of a cube: 0→0, 1→1, 2→8, 3→7, 4→4, 5→5, 6→6, 7→3, 8→2, 9→9. Every digit appears exactly once, so the last digit of a perfect cube tells you the last digit of its cube root.
If a number ends in k zeros, its cube ends in 3k zeros. So a perfect cube ends in 0, 3, 6, 9, ... zeros — a multiple of 3.
Counting cubes by digits: 1-digit cubes are 1 and 8 (2 of them); 2-digit: 27, 64 (2); 3-digit: 125 to 729, i.e. 5³ to 9³ (5); 4-digit: 10³ = 1000 to 21³ = 9261 (12).

ex.q: Find (−0.3)³.
st: Three negative signs multiply to a negative

topics.h: Ramanujan, lying ill, heard that Hardy's taxi number 1729 was 'dull'. He replied at once that it was very interesting! And it has cousins too.
p: Write the cubes 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216 and subtract neighbours: 7, 19, 37, 61, 91. Subtract again: 12, 18, 24, 30. Once more: 6, 6, 6. The third differences of cubes are always 6.
For squares the first differences are the odd numbers 3, 5, 7, 9 and the second differences are always 2. Cube gaps grow much faster than square gaps.
1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³ is the smallest number that is a sum of two cubes in two different ways. Such numbers are called taxicab numbers.
More taxicab numbers: 4104 = 2³ + 16³ = 9³ + 15³ and 13832 = 2³ + 24³ = 18³ + 20³.
Reasoning about cubes: an odd number has an odd cube; a cube ending in 8 has a root ending in 2; the cube of a prime p has exactly 4 factors: 1, p, p², p³.

ex.q: Use differences to find the cube after 216.

topics.rl: Number detectives still hunt for bigger taxicab numbers using computers — a puzzle that began with a taxi ride.

topics.t: Perfect cube test and quick cube roots
topics.h: Someone says 'Find ∛97336!' You can answer 46 in ten seconds — just look at the first and last digits.
p: A number is a perfect cube exactly when every prime in its factorisation appears a multiple of 3 times. 216 = 2³ × 3³ is a cube; 72 = 2³ × 3² is not.
To make a perfect cube, multiply by the primes missing from each group of three, or divide out the leftover primes. 500 = 2² × 5³: multiply by 2 to get 1000, or divide by 4 to get 125.

Quick cube root of a perfect cube up to 6 digits: the last digit of the cube gives the last digit of the root. Strike off the last three digits; the cube that the remaining number just passes gives the tens digit.
Example: 32768 → ends in 8, so the root ends in 2. The front part 32 lies between 27 = 3³ and 64 = 4³, so the tens digit is 3. ∛32768 = 32.

ex.q: Find ∛97336 quickly.
st: Front part 97 lies between 64 = 4³ and 125 = 5³ → tens digit 4

topics.t: A pinch of history: squares and cubes
topics.h: Nearly 4000 years ago, people scratched tables of squares into clay tablets — maths homework that never got lost!
p: Around 1700 BCE, Babylonian scribes made clay tablets listing squares and cubes to speed up their calculations.
In Sanskrit, a square is called varga, a cube is ghana, and the fourth power (the square of a square) is varga-varga.

Aryabhata (around 499 CE) described varga both as a square figure with four equal sides and as the product of two equal numbers. Brahmagupta (7th century CE) wrote down rules for working with squares and square roots.
Indian mathematicians called a square root mula (root of a plant) or pada (foot, base). The idea was carried into Arabic as jidhr and Latin as radix — which is why we still call it a 'root'.

ex.q: What is the varga-varga of 3?
st: varga-varga means the square of a square, the 4th power

topics.rl: When you hear words like 'radical' or 'eradicate' (pull out by the roots), you are hearing the old Latin word radix.

topics.h: Fold a sheet of paper in half again and again. After just 10 folds it would have 1024 layers! Doubling grows faster than you think.
p: In 2⁵, 2 is the base and 5 is the exponent (power). 2⁵ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32.
Each paper fold doubles the layers: after n folds there are 2ⁿ layers.
Powers grow very fast: 2¹⁰ = 1024 is much bigger than 10² = 100, even though both use a 2 and a 10.
A negative base with an even exponent gives a positive answer: (−2)⁴ = 16. With an odd exponent it stays negative: (−2)³ = −8.
(−1) to an even power is 1; (−1) to an odd power is −1.

ex.q: Write 1,00,000 as a power of 10 and 81 as a power of 3.

topics.t: Folding paper: the power of doubling
topics.h: Fold a thin sheet of paper in half 46 times (if you could!) and the pile would stretch past the Moon. Doubling is that powerful.
p: Every fold doubles the thickness. If the sheet starts t thick, after n folds it is t × 2ⁿ thick.
10 folds multiply the thickness by 2¹⁰ = 1024. A sheet 0.001 cm thick becomes about 1 cm thick.

After 30 folds the same sheet would be 0.001 × 2³⁰ cm ≈ 10.7 km tall — far taller than the Burj Khalifa (about 828 m) and even Mount Everest. After 46 folds it would be about 7 lakh km, more than the Earth–Moon distance (about 3,84,000 km).
Adding the same amount each time is linear growth: 2, 4, 6, 8, ... Multiplying by the same amount is exponential growth: 2, 4, 8, 16, ... Exponential growth soon leaves linear growth far behind.
A ladder to the Moon with 1 m steps would need 38,40,00,000 steps, but doubling gets there in fewer than 50 folds.

ex.q: A card 0.01 cm thick is folded 5 times. How thick is the pile?
st: Each fold doubles: 5 folds multiply by 2⁵ = 32

topics.h: Can you work out 2²⁰ ÷ 2¹⁸ in one second? With the laws of exponents, you can: it is just 2² = 4!
p: Same base, multiply → add the exponents: aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ. So 3² × 3⁴ = 3⁶.
Same base, divide → subtract the exponents: aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ. So 7⁹ ÷ 7⁴ = 7⁵.
Power of a power → multiply the exponents: (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ. So (5²)³ = 5⁶.
Same exponent: aᵐ × bᵐ = (ab)ᵐ. So 2³ × 5³ = 10³ = 1000.
Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1, and a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ. So 9⁰ = 1 and 2⁻³ = 1/8.

ex.q: Simplify (2⁵ × 2³) ÷ 2⁶.

topics.rl: Scientists and computer engineers use these laws every day, for example to say that 2¹⁰ × 2¹⁰ bytes is 2²⁰ bytes (about one million).

topics.h: What is the last digit of 2¹⁰⁰? Nobody multiplies it out — a repeating pattern tells you in seconds.
p: Prime factorisations look neat with exponents: 32400 = 2⁴ × 3⁴ × 5², and 720 = 2⁴ × 3² × 5.
Same exponent, dividing: mᵃ ÷ nᵃ = (m ÷ n)ᵃ. So 15³ ÷ 5³ = 3³ = 27.
Change bases to match: 4 = 2², 8 = 2³, 9 = 3², 27 = 3³. So 8⁴ ÷ 4⁵ = 2¹² ÷ 2¹⁰ = 2² = 4.

Units digits of powers repeat: powers of 2 end in 2, 4, 8, 6, 2, 4, ... (a cycle of 4). So 2¹⁰⁰ ends in 6, since 100 is a multiple of 4. Powers of 3 end in 3, 9, 7, 1; powers of 4 in 4, 6; powers of 9 in 9, 1.

ex.q: Simplify 8⁴ ÷ 4⁵.

topics.t: Powers in stories: tripling, doubling and counting choices
topics.h: How many number plates can India make with just 2 letters and 4 digits? Over 67 lakh — and powers tell you why.
p: Repeated tripling: if shining stones triple every day starting from 1, there are 1, 3, 9, 27, ... — 3ⁿ stones after n days.

Magical pond: if lotuses double every day and cover the pond on day 30, they covered half of it on day 29. If fish double for 5 days and then triple for 3 days, their number is multiplied by 2⁵ × 3³ = 864.
Multiplication principle: 3 shirts and 4 pants make 3 × 4 = 12 outfits. A 3-digit lock using 0–9 has 10 × 10 × 10 = 10³ = 1000 codes.
Number plates with 2 letters then 4 digits: 26² × 10⁴ = 67,60,000 plates.
To give unique codes to many items, find the smallest power that is big enough: 5000 students need 4-digit codes, since 10³ = 1000 is too few but 10⁴ = 10000 is enough.

ex.q: How many 4-digit PINs can be made from the digits 0–9?
st: Each of the 4 places has 10 choices

topics.rl: Every UPI PIN, phone number and vehicle number in India is designed using this multiplication principle.

rv.summary: Repeated doubling or tripling gives powers: tripling from 1 gives 3ⁿ after n days. The multiplication principle counts choices by multiplying, so a 3-digit lock has 10³ = 1000 codes.

topics.t: Zero and negative exponents, and power lines
topics.h: Cut a 1 m ribbon in half, then half again, and again... The pieces are 2⁻¹, 2⁻², 2⁻³ metres long. Yes — negative powers are real!
p: Going down the powers of 2 divides by 2 each step: 2³ = 8, 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2, 2⁰ = 1, 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁻² = 1/4. Halving a 1 m strip again and again gives these lengths.
So n⁰ = 1 for any n that is not 0, and n⁻ᵃ = 1/nᵃ. 0⁰ is not given a value this way, because getting it from 0ᵃ ÷ 0ᵃ would mean dividing by 0.
Power line: mark 4⁻², 4⁻¹, 4⁰, 4¹, 4², 4³ at equal steps. Multiplying by 4² means moving 2 steps right; dividing by 4³ means moving 3 steps left.
All the laws work for every integer exponent: 5⁻³ × 5⁵ = 5², (2⁻²)³ = 2⁻⁶, and 3⁴ ÷ 3⁷ = 3⁻³ = 1/27.

ex.q: Simplify (2⁻³ × 2⁵) ÷ 2⁻¹.

topics.rl: Scientists write tiny sizes with negative powers: a hair is about 10⁻⁴ m thick.

topics.t: Powers of 10: expanded form and big-number names
topics.h: 1 arab = 1 billion = 100 crore. Same number, three names! Powers of 10 help us switch between them.
p: Expanded form with powers of 10: 4705 = 4 × 10³ + 7 × 10² + 0 × 10¹ + 5 × 10⁰.
Decimal places use negative powers: 23.56 = 2 × 10¹ + 3 × 10⁰ + 5 × 10⁻¹ + 6 × 10⁻².
Indian names: lakh = 10⁵, crore = 10⁷, arab = 10⁹, kharab = 10¹¹. International names: thousand = 10³, million = 10⁶, billion = 10⁹.
So 1 million = 10 lakh, 1 crore = 10 million, and 1 billion = 1 arab = 100 crore.
A googol is 10¹⁰⁰ — 1 followed by 100 zeros. A googolplex is 10 to the power googol: 1 followed by a googol zeros, far too many ever to write down.

ex.q: Write 50,306.07 in expanded form with powers of 10.

topics.rl: News reports switch between '₹1 lakh crore' and '₹1 trillion' — both are 10¹² rupees.

topics.h: The Sun is about 15,00,00,000 km away. Counting those zeros is tiring! Scientists simply write 1.5 × 10⁸ km.
p: Scientific notation (standard form) writes a number as a × 10ⁿ, where a is at least 1 and less than 10.
For a big number, move the decimal point left and count the jumps: 4,50,000 = 4.5 × 10⁵.
For a tiny number, move the decimal point right; the exponent becomes negative: 0.0005 = 5 × 10⁻⁴.
To compare two numbers in standard form, compare the powers of 10 first: 2 × 10⁸ is bigger than 9 × 10⁷.

topics.t: Estimating big numbers and big times
topics.h: Have you lived for a billion seconds? Not yet — you would need to be about 32 years old!
p: To estimate: (1) make a guess, (2) choose simple assumptions (a model), (3) calculate, (4) check whether the answer makes sense.
Tulabhara-style problems: a person is balanced against coins, fruits or grain. A 60 kg person = 60,000 g. If each coin weighs about 5 g, that is 60,000 ÷ 5 = 12,000 coins.
Time in powers of 10: 1 day = 86,400 s (about 10⁵ s); 10⁶ s ≈ 11.6 days; 1 year ≈ 3.15 × 10⁷ s; 10⁹ s ≈ 31.7 years.
A 13-year-old has lived about 13 × 365 = 4745 days ≈ 1,13,880 hours ≈ 4.1 × 10⁸ seconds.
Big counts become easy to compare as powers of 10: India's population is about 1.4 × 10⁹; a 10-litre bucket holds about 2 × 10⁵ drops if one drop is 0.05 ml.

ex.q: At a tulabhara, a 50 kg child is balanced with bananas of about 125 g each. About how many bananas are needed?

topics.rl: Planners estimate how many buses a festival needs or how much water a city drinks using the same guess–model–compute–check idea.

topics.t: A pinch of history: Indian names for huge numbers
topics.h: Long before calculators, Indian texts had names for numbers with 50 zeros. Ancient India loved big numbers!
p: Ancient Indian texts gave names to very large powers of ten, far beyond what daily life needed.
In the Buddhist text Lalitavistara, young Siddhartha names number after number, each 100 times the one before, going far beyond a koti (crore) up to tallakshana = 10⁵³.

Jaina and Pali (Buddhist) works use enormous numbers to describe time and the universe. Mahaviracharya (9th century CE), in his book Ganita Sara Sangraha, listed 24 names for the powers of ten one after another, from eka (1) up to 10²³.
Modern Indian names continue the lakh–crore pattern, each 100 times the last: arab 10⁹, kharab 10¹¹, neel 10¹³, padma 10¹⁵, shankh 10¹⁷, maha shankh 10¹⁹.

ex.q: How many crore make 1 padma?

topics.rl: Words like padma and shankh still appear in Indian number charts and quiz shows.

topics.t: Power puzzles: compare, always or never
topics.h: Which is bigger, 4³ or 3⁴? 2⁸ or 8²? Guess first — the answers surprise many grown-ups!
p: Compare by working them out: 4³ = 64 but 3⁴ = 81; 2⁸ = 256 but 8² = 64; and 2⁴ = 4² = 16 is a rare tie.
Always, sometimes or never? 'An odd number to any power is odd' is always true. 'aⁿ is bigger than a' is only sometimes true (false for a = 1). '2ⁿ ends in 0' is never true.
Numbers that are both perfect squares and perfect cubes are sixth powers: 1, 64 (= 8² = 4³), 729 (= 27² = 9³), 4096, ...
In a 'make the biggest number' game with digits and powers, a bigger exponent usually helps more than a bigger base: 3⁵ = 243 beats 5³ = 125, and 9⁹ is far bigger than 99.

ex.q: Which is larger: 2¹⁰ or 10³?

topics.t: Why and how people first counted
topics.h: A shepherd long ago could not count to 50 — yet she always knew if a goat went missing. How?
p: Early people counted to keep track of their animals, food stores and trade, and to follow days and seasons (when to sow, when to harvest).
Counting is one-to-one matching: put one pebble aside for each goat in the morning. In the evening, take one pebble back for each goat. Pebbles left over mean goats are missing.
People counted with sticks or pebbles, with spoken sounds (say a, b, c, ... as number names) and with written marks. Each has limits: big numbers need too many pebbles, and 26 letters soon run out.
A numeral is a symbol (or group of symbols) that stands for a number, like 7 or VII. A number system is a set of numerals with rules for writing and reading every number.
You can design your own system: if ★ means 10 and • means 1, then ★★•••• is 24.

ex.q: Leela puts aside one pebble for each of her 23 goats in the morning. In the evening each returning goat takes away one pebble, and 2 pebbles are left. How many goats returned?
st: 2 pebbles left → 2 goats did not return

topics.rl: A school bus conductor ticking each child's name on a list is doing one-to-one matching too.

topics.t: How Indian numerals reached the world
topics.h: The digits 0 to 9 on every phone in the world began their journey in India. Why do some people still call them 'Arabic'?
p: The Yajurveda lists names for powers of ten: eka (1), dasha (10), shata (100), sahasra (1000), ayuta (10⁴), niyuta (10⁵), prayuta (10⁶), arbuda (10⁷), ... up to parardha (10¹²).

The ten digits 0–9 with place value grew in India. The Bakhshali manuscript, found in 1881 in a village now in Pakistan, uses a dot for zero. Aryabhata (499 CE) explained that each place is ten times the one before.
In the 9th century CE, Al-Khwarizmi and Al-Kindi in Baghdad wrote books on calculating with Indian numerals. In 1202 CE Fibonacci's book Liber Abaci spread them across Europe.

So the name 'Arabic numerals' is misleading: they began in India and travelled through the Arab world. 'Hindu-Arabic numerals' or 'Indian numerals' is more accurate — Arab scholars themselves called them Indian numbers.

ex.q: How many sahasra make one ayuta?

topics.rl: Every price tag, cricket score and phone number you read uses this Indian invention.

topics.t: Early counting: bones, body parts and twos
topics.h: One of the oldest maths objects ever found is a baboon bone with 29 scratches — over 40,000 years old!
p: Some communities in Papua New Guinea count by touching body parts in a fixed order — fingers, then wrist, elbow, shoulder, ear, eye and so on. Each body part stands for a number.

Tally marks on bones: the Lebombo bone from the Lebombo mountains of southern Africa (more than 40,000 years old) has 29 notches. The Ishango bone from Congo in Africa (more than 20,000 years old) has groups of notches.
The Gumulgal people of Australia counted in twos with just two words: urapon (1) and ukasar (2). So 3 = ukasar-urapon, 4 = ukasar-ukasar, 5 = ukasar-ukasar-urapon.
Most people can see how many things there are at a glance only up to about 4 or 5. Beyond that we must count or group — which is why tallies are bundled in fives.

ex.q: In a made-up body-count: little finger 1, ring finger 2, middle 3, index 4, thumb 5, wrist 6, elbow 7, shoulder 8. Which body part means 7?

topics.rl: When a cricket umpire counts balls in an over on his fingers, he is using body parts to count.

topics.t: Counting long ago: tallies, Egyptian and Roman numerals
topics.h: Long before anyone wrote the digit 7, a shepherd tied a knot in a rope or scratched a mark on a bone for every sheep that went out to graze.
p: The first counting was one-to-one matching: one pebble, knot or tally mark for each object.
Grouping makes counting faster. Tally marks are bundled in fives, so 3 bundles and 2 marks means 17.
Egyptian numerals used a picture for each power of ten: a stroke for 1, a heel bone for 10, a coiled rope for 100 and a lotus flower for 1000. You repeat the pictures and add.
Roman numerals use I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1000. A smaller symbol written before a bigger one is subtracted: IV = 4, XL = 40, XC = 90, CM = 900.
These systems have no place value and no zero, so big numbers need many symbols and sums like 347 × 26 become very hard.

ex.q: Write 1984 in Roman numerals.

topics.rl: Clock towers, chapter numbers in old books and 'Class VIII' written on your notebook all use Roman numerals.

topics.t: Roman sums, the abacus and Egyptian limits
topics.h: Try multiplying CCCXLVII by XXVI. Hard? The Romans thought so too — that is why they used counting boards!
p: Adding Roman numerals means putting the symbols together and regrouping: XXVII + XIV = 27 + 14 = 41 = XLI.
Multiplying Roman numerals is very clumsy, because there is no place value and the symbols do not line up in columns.
Roman numerals can be long: 3888 = MMMDCCCLXXXVIII uses 15 symbols, but our system needs only 4 digits. Our system is far more efficient.
A decimal abacus has lines for 1, 10, 100, 1000, ... and counters on them. When a line gets 10 counters, remove them and put 1 counter on the next line up.
The Egyptian system needs a brand-new symbol for every new power of ten, so bigger and bigger numbers need ever more symbols.

st: Ones: 6 + 7 = 13 → leave 3, carry 1 counter to tens

topics.h: Imagine a world where people have only 4 fingers. They would write 16 as '100'! Let's visit some other bases.
p: In a base-5 landmark system, the landmarks are 1, 5, 25, 125, 625, ... — each 5 times the one before. In base n, the landmarks are 1, n, n², n³, ...
Adding with regrouping: in base 5, five of one landmark make one of the next. 4 ones + 3 ones = 7 ones = 1 five and 2 ones.
Multiplying landmarks gives a landmark: 25 × 125 = 5² × 5³ = 5⁵ = 3125. Multiplying by the base moves every symbol up one landmark — like putting a 0 at the end.
Base 8 uses digits 0–7 and places 1, 8, 64, 512. So 100 = 1 × 64 + 4 × 8 + 4 = 144 in base 8.

ex.q: Add 34 (base 5) and 23 (base 5).

topics.h: Computers count with only two digits, 0 and 1. To a computer, 1010 means ten!
p: The base tells how many make one group before you move to the next place. Base 10 groups in tens, base 5 in fives and base 2 in twos.
In base 2 (binary) the place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ... So 1011 in base 2 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.
In base 5 the place values are 1, 5, 25, 125, ... and only the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 are used.
To write a number in base 2, break it into place values: 13 = 8 + 4 + 1, so 13 = 1101 in base 2.
Base 10 probably comes from our ten fingers, and base 60 still lives on in hours, minutes and seconds.

topics.h: Why does an hour have 60 minutes and not 100? Blame (or thank!) the Mesopotamians of 4000 years ago.
p: The Mesopotamians (Babylonians) pressed wedge marks into clay: a thin wedge for 1 and a corner wedge for 10. Each place could hold any amount up to 59.
Their places stand for 1, 60, 60² = 3600, ... So '2 | 15' means 2 × 60 + 15 = 135.

Why 60? One idea: 60 has many factors (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, 30, 60), so halves, thirds, quarters and fifths are easy. Another: count the 12 finger segments of one hand with the thumb, and keep track on the 5 fingers of the other hand: 12 × 5 = 60.
Regroup at 60: 60 ones make one 60, and 60 sixties make one 3600.
At first they left a blank space for an empty place, which was confusing — '1  1' could be 61 or 3601. Later scribes used a special placeholder sign.

traps: Don't read the places as tens and hundreds
Don't put 60 or more in one place; a place holds at most 59
Don't read '1  1' as only 61: without a placeholder it could also be 3601

topics.t: Maya numbers, Chinese rods and the road to zero
topics.h: The Maya drew a shell for zero, and Chinese scholars counted with bamboo rods. Each idea was a step towards our 0–9 system.
p: Maya numbers use a dot for 1, a bar for 5 and a shell for 0. So 3 bars and 4 dots = 15 + 4 = 19.
Maya places are stacked from the bottom up and stand for 1, 20, 360 (= 18 × 20, linked to their calendar), 7200, ...

Chinese rod numerals are base 10 with place value. Ones, hundreds and ten-thousands use vertical rods (zong); tens and thousands use horizontal rods (heng). Alternating stops neighbouring digits from running together; an empty place was left blank.

The big story: one-to-one tallies → grouping → special symbols for groups (landmarks) → landmarks as powers of a base → place value → zero as a digit and as a number. The Indian system has every step.

ex.q: A Maya number has 1 dot in the 360s place, a shell in the 20s place and 2 bars in the ones place. What is it?

topics.rl: Ruins of Maya cities in Central America still have carved numbers in dots and bars for dates.

rv.summary: Maya numbers use a dot for 1, a bar for 5 and a shell for 0, with places 1, 20, 360, 7200. Chinese rod numerals are base 10, switching vertical and horizontal rods. The Indian system completes the path to place value with zero.
focus: Read Maya digits and multi-place Maya numbers
Know the Maya place values 1, 20, 360, 7200
Know how Chinese rod numerals alternate rods
Order the steps in the story of number systems
remember: Maya: dot 1, bar 5, shell 0
Chinese rods: ones vertical (zong), tens horizontal (heng), alternating
Tally → grouping → landmarks → bases → place value → zero
traps: The Maya third place is 360, not 400
Don't count bars and dots as 1 each: a bar is 5
Zero as a digit came last, not early

topics.t: Place value and the story of zero
topics.h: With just ten symbols, 0 to 9, you can write any number you can imagine. The secret? Place value, and a humble little zero.
p: In a place value system, a digit's value depends on its position. In 555 the three 5s mean 500, 50 and 5.
Our system is base 10: each place is worth 10 times the place on its right (ones, tens, hundreds, thousands...).
Zero is a placeholder: 205 and 25 are different numbers because the 0 keeps the tens place empty.
About 4000 years ago the Babylonians used place value with base 60. The Maya of Central America used base 20 and drew a shell for zero.
Indian mathematicians built the base-10 system with zero as a number. Brahmagupta (7th century CE) wrote rules like a + 0 = a and a − a = 0. These numerals travelled through the Arab world to Europe.

ex.q: Write 40,305 in expanded form using powers of 10.
st: Zeros add nothing, but they keep the other digits in their places

topics.rl: Every price tag, PIN code and cricket score uses place value. One extra zero turns a ₹500 note into ₹5000!

rv.summary: In a place value system a digit's value depends on its position, and in base 10 each place is 10 times the one on its right. Zero holds empty places, and Indian mathematicians like Brahmagupta treated zero as a number.
focus: Find the value of a digit from its place
Write numbers in expanded form with powers of 10
Explain why zero is needed as a placeholder
Read Babylonian (base 60) and Maya (base 20) place values
remember: Each place is 10 times the place on its right
Zero keeps empty places: 205 ≠ 25
Babylonians: base 60; Maya: base 20 with a shell for zero
Brahmagupta (7th century CE): a + 0 = a and a − a = 0
traps: Don't forget zeros for empty places: five thousand and seven is 5007
Don't misread places with Indian commas: in 4,60,213 the 6 is 60,000
Don't read base-60 or base-20 digits as base 10

topics.h: The blackboard, your maths notebook, a door, and the paper kite you fly on Makar Sankranti are all quadrilaterals. But they are not all the same kind!
p: A quadrilateral is a closed figure with 4 straight sides, 4 vertices, 4 angles and 2 diagonals.
A trapezium has a pair of parallel sides. A parallelogram has both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
A rectangle is a parallelogram with all four angles 90°. A rhombus is a parallelogram with all four sides equal.
A square has all sides equal and all angles 90°, so every square is a rectangle and also a rhombus.
A kite has two pairs of equal sides, and each pair sits next to each other (adjacent).

ex.q: A quadrilateral has all four sides 5 cm, and one of its angles is 90°. Which quadrilateral is it?
st: All sides equal, so it is a rhombus, which is a parallelogram
In a parallelogram, opposite angles are equal and neighbouring angles add to 180°
So one 90° angle makes all four angles 90°
All sides equal and all angles 90° means a square

topics.rl: Carpenters check that a door frame is a true rectangle, and rangoli makers love rhombus and kite patterns.

rv.summary: A quadrilateral has 4 sides, 4 angles and 2 diagonals. Trapeziums have a pair of parallel sides, parallelograms have two pairs, and rectangles, rhombuses and squares are special parallelograms; a kite has two pairs of equal neighbouring sides.
focus: Name quadrilaterals from their sides and angles
Know which shapes are special cases of others
Find perimeters of kites and rhombuses
Find a missing angle using the 360° sum
remember: Trapezium: a pair of parallel sides; parallelogram: both pairs
Rectangle: parallelogram with all angles 90°; rhombus: parallelogram with all sides equal
Square: all sides equal and all angles 90° (a rectangle and a rhombus)
Kite: two pairs of equal sides next to each other
traps: Every square is a rhombus, but not every rhombus is a square
Right angles alone don't make a square: check the sides
Angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°, not 180°

topics.h: Start with just one rule — 'all four angles are right angles' — and you can prove everything else about a rectangle. Like a detective!
p: Definition: a rectangle is a quadrilateral with four right angles. Everything else is deduced from this.
Opposite sides are parallel: the two angles on one side add to 90° + 90° = 180°, and when co-interior angles add to 180°, the lines are parallel.
Opposite sides are equal: the diagonal AC splits rectangle ABCD into triangles ABC and CDA, which are congruent (AC is common and the alternate angles are equal). So AB = CD and BC = DA.
If a quadrilateral has three right angles, the fourth is 360° − 270° = 90°, so it must be a rectangle.
The diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so OA = OB = OC = OD. That makes triangles like AOB isosceles — handy for finding angles.

ex.q: In rectangle ABCD the diagonals meet at O and ∠OAB = 30°. Find ∠OBA and ∠AOB.

topics.rl: Carpenters check a door frame is a true rectangle by measuring both diagonals — if they are equal, the corners are right angles.

rv.summary: A rectangle is defined as a quadrilateral with four right angles, and its other properties are proved from this. Its opposite sides are parallel and equal, and its diagonals are equal and bisect each other, making isosceles triangles.
focus: Prove opposite sides of a rectangle are parallel and equal
Show that three right angles force the fourth
Use OA = OB = OC = OD to find angles at the diagonals
Find diagonal lengths from half-diagonals
remember: Rectangle: a quadrilateral with four right angles
Co-interior angles 90° + 90° = 180° → opposite sides parallel
Diagonal AC gives congruent triangles ABC and CDA → opposite sides equal
Diagonals are equal and bisect each other: OA = OB = OC = OD
traps: The diagonals of a rectangle do not always meet at 90°
A diagonal does not bisect the right angle of a rectangle
Don't stop at half the diagonal when asked for the full one

topics.h: Cross two sticks, join their ends with a thread — and you have made a quadrilateral. Which one? It depends on how you cross the sticks!
p: Two equal lines that bisect each other (at any angle) give a rectangle when their ends are joined. Two equal sticks tied at their midpoints with a thread around the ends make a right angle at every corner.
Draw two perpendicular diameters of a circle and join their ends: you get a square, because the diagonals are equal, bisect each other and meet at 90°.
Any two lines that bisect each other give a parallelogram. If they bisect each other at right angles (but are unequal), you get a rhombus.
Kite from its diagonals: make one diagonal the perpendicular bisector of the other, but do not cut the first one in half.
Square from one diagonal, without a protractor: draw diagonal AC, construct its perpendicular bisector with a compass, then mark B and D on it at a distance of half of AC from the centre.

ex.q: Diagonals of 8 cm and 8 cm bisect each other at 50°. Which quadrilateral do you get?
st: So it is a rectangle (not a square)

topics.rl: Kite makers tie two sticks in a cross before pasting the paper — how they cross them decides the shape of the kite!

rv.summary: The diagonals decide the shape: lines that bisect each other give a parallelogram, equal ones a rectangle, perpendicular ones a rhombus, and equal perpendicular ones a square. A kite has one diagonal as the perpendicular bisector of the other.
focus: Name the quadrilateral formed from given diagonals
Build a square from perpendicular diameters of a circle
Construct a square from one diagonal without a protractor
Build a kite from its diagonals
remember: Bisect each other → parallelogram
Equal and bisect each other → rectangle
Bisect each other at 90° → rhombus; also equal → square
Kite: one diagonal is the perpendicular bisector of the other
traps: Perpendicular diagonals alone don't make a square: they must also be equal
A rectangle needs equal diagonals; unequal ones never make one
Don't think both diagonals of a kite are cut in half; only one is

topics.h: Draw any quadrilateral at all, even a wonky one. Tear off its four corners and put them together: they always make a full turn of 360°!
p: The angles of every quadrilateral add up to 360°, because a diagonal splits it into two triangles: 180° + 180°.
Rectangle: the diagonals are equal and bisect each other.
Rhombus: the diagonals bisect each other at right angles (they are perpendicular), and each diagonal bisects the angles at its ends.
Square: the diagonals are equal, perpendicular and bisect each other. It has every property of a rectangle and a rhombus.
Kite: the diagonals are perpendicular, and one diagonal cuts the other in half.

ex.q: The angles of a quadrilateral are x, 2x, 3x and 4x. Find each angle.

topics.rl: Tile makers and architects use the 360° rule to check that floor tiles and window frames fit together with no gaps.

rv.summary: The angles of any quadrilateral add up to 360°, since a diagonal splits it into two triangles. Rectangles have equal diagonals that bisect each other, rhombuses have perpendicular ones that bisect each other, and squares have both.
focus: Find missing angles using the 360° sum
Solve angle problems like x, 2x, 3x, 4x
Use diagonal properties of rectangles, rhombuses, squares and kites
Use the fact that a rhombus diagonal bisects its angles
remember: Angle sum of a quadrilateral = 360° (180° + 180°)
Rectangle: diagonals equal and bisect each other
Rhombus: diagonals bisect each other at 90° and bisect the angles
Square: diagonals equal, perpendicular and bisect each other
traps: Don't stop at x: find the angle asked for
Equal diagonals is not the same as bisecting each other
Perpendicular, bisecting but unequal diagonals give a rhombus, not a square or kite

topics.h: Push a rectangular photo frame from one corner and it leans over, but its opposite sides stay parallel. You have made a parallelogram!
p: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal and parallel.
Opposite angles are equal.
Neighbouring (adjacent) angles add up to 180°.
The diagonals bisect each other: they cut each other exactly in half. They are not always equal.
Why? A diagonal splits a parallelogram into two identical (congruent) triangles.

ex.q: In parallelogram PQRS, ∠P = 70°. Find ∠Q, ∠R and ∠S.

topics.rl: Folding stools, car jacks and the scissor-lift used to fix street lights all use parallelograms that change shape but keep opposite sides parallel.

rv.summary: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal and parallel, opposite angles are equal and neighbouring angles add up to 180°. The diagonals bisect each other but are not always equal.
focus: Find all angles of a parallelogram from one angle
Use ratios or expressions for neighbouring angles
Use the fact that diagonals bisect each other
Find the perimeter of a parallelogram
remember: Opposite sides are equal and parallel
Opposite angles are equal
Neighbouring angles add up to 180°
The diagonals bisect each other
traps: Opposite angles are equal; they do not add up to 180°
The diagonals of a parallelogram are not always equal
Neighbouring angles add to 180°, not 360°

topics.h: Take two identical paper triangles and slide them together. You can make a rectangle, a kite or a parallelogram — depending on how you join them!
p: On a geoboard (pins in a square grid), rubber bands make squares, rectangles, parallelograms, kites and trapeziums. Tilted squares can be made too.
To find the area of a tilted shape on a geoboard, draw a box around it and subtract the corner triangles.
Two congruent right triangles joined along the longest side: turned half-way round, they make a rectangle; as mirror images, they make a kite.
Two congruent triangles joined along any side, one turned half-way round, always make a parallelogram.
Joining the midpoints of the sides of a square gives a smaller, tilted square with exactly half the area.

ex.q: A square has side 10 cm. Its side midpoints are joined. What is the area of the new square?
st: The four corner triangles together make half of it

topics.rl: Tile and rangoli designs often use squares inside squares made by joining midpoints.

rv.summary: Quadrilaterals can be explored on a geoboard and by joining congruent triangles. Two congruent triangles joined with one turned half-way round make a parallelogram, and joining the midpoints of a square gives a tilted square with half the area.
focus: Find areas of tilted shapes on a geoboard by boxing and subtracting
Predict shapes made by joining two congruent triangles
Find the area of the midpoint square
Make squares, rectangles and kites on a geoboard
remember: Two right triangles on their longest side: turned → rectangle; mirrored → kite
Two congruent triangles, one turned half-way round → parallelogram
Midpoint square of a square has half the area
Tilted area = box area − corner triangles
traps: The midpoint square has half the area, not a quarter
Don't expect turning and flipping to give the same shape
Don't count only whole squares inside a tilted shape

topics.h: The kite you fly at Makar Sankranti and the trapezium-shaped dhol stand both have their own special rules. Let's discover them!
p: A kite ABCD has two pairs of equal neighbouring sides: AB = AD and CB = CD.
In a kite, the diagonal AC (joining the corners where equal sides meet) is the perpendicular bisector of the other diagonal BD. Also ∠B = ∠D.
A trapezium has at least one pair of parallel sides. If AB ∥ DC, the two angles on each slanting side add to 180°: ∠A + ∠D = 180° and ∠B + ∠C = 180°.
An isosceles trapezium has its non-parallel sides equal. Its base angles are equal (∠A = ∠B and ∠C = ∠D), and its diagonals are equal.

ex.q: In trapezium ABCD, AB ∥ DC and ∠A = 65°. Find ∠D.
st: ∠A and ∠D are on the same slanting side
They are co-interior angles, so they add to 180°

topics.rl: Many bridges and the sides of a handbag are trapeziums; festival kites are, of course, kites!

rv.summary: A kite has two pairs of equal neighbouring sides; one diagonal is the perpendicular bisector of the other and the angles between the unequal sides are equal. In a trapezium, the angles on each slanting side add to 180°.
focus: Find angles and lengths in a kite
Know which kite diagonal is bisected
Find angles in trapeziums using co-interior angles
Use the properties of an isosceles trapezium
remember: Kite ABCD (AB = AD, CB = CD): AC is the perpendicular bisector of BD; ∠B = ∠D
Trapezium with AB ∥ DC: ∠A + ∠D = 180° and ∠B + ∠C = 180°
Isosceles trapezium: equal base angles and equal diagonals
traps: A kite's diagonals do not bisect each other
The angles on a slanting side of a trapezium add to 180°; they are not equal
Don't count only one of the equal slanting sides in the perimeter

topics.h: Is a square a kite? Is a rhombus a parallelogram? Quadrilaterals have a family tree, and some shapes belong to many families at once!
p: Family links: every square is a rectangle and a rhombus; every rectangle and every rhombus is a parallelogram; every rhombus (so every square) is also a kite.
In a Venn diagram, the squares sit where the rectangles and rhombuses overlap, all inside the parallelograms; the rhombuses also sit inside the kites.

Judge by diagonals: bisect each other → parallelogram; equal and bisect each other → rectangle; bisect each other at 90° → rhombus; both → square; one is the perpendicular bisector of the other → kite.
If both pairs of opposite angles are equal, the shape is a parallelogram. Perpendicular diagonals alone do NOT make a rhombus — a kite has them too.

Proof: if AB = CD and BC = DA, draw diagonal AC. Triangles ABC and CDA are congruent (SSS), so ∠BAC = ∠DCA. These are alternate angles, so AB ∥ DC; in the same way AD ∥ BC. So the shape is a parallelogram.

ex.q: A rectangle has two neighbouring sides equal. What is it?
st: A rectangle has 4 right angles and opposite sides equal
Neighbouring sides equal → all four sides equal
4 equal sides and 4 right angles → square

topics.rl: Sorting shapes into families is like sorting cousins and siblings in a family tree at a wedding!

rv.summary: Quadrilaterals form a family: squares are rectangles and rhombuses, rectangles and rhombuses are parallelograms, and rhombuses are kites. Diagonal and angle properties tell you which family member a shape is.
focus: Decide which family statements are true
Place shapes in a Venn diagram of quadrilaterals
Identify a shape from its diagonal properties
Prove that equal opposite sides make a parallelogram (SSS)
remember: Every square is a rectangle and a rhombus; every rhombus is a kite
Equal diagonals that bisect each other → rectangle
Both pairs of opposite angles equal → parallelogram
Opposite sides equal: diagonal gives congruent triangles (SSS), alternate angles → parallel sides
traps: Perpendicular diagonals alone do not make a rhombus: a kite has them too
A kite is not always a parallelogram
Don't reverse a family link: not every rectangle is a square

topics.h: 15 = 7 + 8 = 4 + 5 + 6 = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5. Three ways! But try as hard as you like — you can never do it for 16.
p: Many numbers can be written as a sum of two or more consecutive natural numbers: 9 = 4 + 5 = 2 + 3 + 4, and 15 has three such ways.
Every odd number above 1 works with two terms: 2k + 1 = k + (k + 1). Powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, ...) can never be written this way.
Algebra for consecutive numbers: n, n + 1, n + 2 add to 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1). If the greatest is m, the three numbers are m − 2, m − 1, m, with sum 3m − 3.
Putting + or − between 1, 2, 3, ..., k: changing a + to a − changes the total by an even amount, so every result has the same parity (odd or even) as 1 + 2 + ... + k.

ex.q: Write 18 as a sum of consecutive numbers in two ways.

topics.rl: Seating rows in a stadium often grow by one seat each row — totals of such rows are sums of consecutive numbers.

rv.summary: Many numbers are sums of consecutive natural numbers: every odd number above 1 is k + (k + 1), but powers of 2 can never be written this way. Algebra like n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 3n + 3 helps find the numbers.
focus: Write numbers as sums of consecutive numbers in different ways
Know which numbers (powers of 2) cannot be written this way
Use algebra for the sum of consecutive numbers
Use parity to decide which +/− results are possible
remember: Powers of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, ...) are never sums of consecutive numbers
n + (n + 1) + (n + 2) = 3(n + 1); with greatest m: 3m − 3
Changing a + to a − changes the total by an even amount
traps: Don't give the middle number when the largest is asked
Even numbers can often be written this way (18 = 5 + 6 + 7); only powers of 2 can't
Don't count up from the greatest number m; the numbers are m − 2, m − 1, m

topics.h: Pick any 2-digit number, reverse its digits and subtract the smaller from the larger. Your friend can bet the answer is in the 9 times table, every single time!
p: Parity means odd or even. Even + even = even, odd + odd = even, odd + even = odd, odd × odd = odd.
The sum of any 3 consecutive numbers is 3 times the middle one: (n − 1) + n + (n + 1) = 3n.
Triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, ... are sums 1 + 2 + ... + n, and equal n(n + 1) ÷ 2.
The reverse-and-subtract trick: (10a + b) − (10b + a) = 9(a − b), so the answer is always a multiple of 9.
In a cryptarithm, letters stand for digits. Use carries, last digits and parity to crack it.

ex.q: In the puzzle A + A + A = BA, each letter is a different digit. Find A and B.
st: 3 × A ends in the digit A, so 2 × A must end in 0
A = 0 gives 0 + 0 + 0 = 0, which is not a 2-digit number

topics.rl: Puzzle pages in newspapers, Sudoku and magic tricks at a Diwali party all use these number patterns.

rv.summary: Parity rules (odd + odd = even, odd × odd = odd) and algebra explain number tricks. Three consecutive numbers add to 3 times the middle one, triangular numbers are n(n + 1) ÷ 2, and reverse-and-subtract always gives a multiple of 9.
focus: Use parity to decide if sums and products are odd or even
Find consecutive numbers from their sum
Find triangular numbers and sums 1 + 2 + ... + n
Solve cryptarithms using place value and carries
remember: Even + even = even, odd + odd = even, odd + even = odd, odd × odd = odd
traps: Don't forget to divide by 2: 1 + ... + 50 = 1275, not 2550
In a cryptarithm, 4A is a 2-digit number, not 4 × A
The sum of 4 consecutive numbers is not always a multiple of 4 (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10)

topics.t: Parity puzzles: always, sometimes or never
topics.h: Can five odd numbers add up to 30? Before you try 100 combinations, parity tells you the answer in one line.
p: 2n is always even and 2n + 1 is always odd. n² has the same parity as n.
n(n + 1) is always even, because one of two consecutive numbers is even. So n² + n is always even.
An odd count of odd numbers always adds to an odd number; an even count adds to an even number. So five odd numbers can never make 30.

Pairs to make fours: split even numbers into multiples of 4 (4, 8, 12, ...) and the rest (2, 6, 10, ..., which leave remainder 2). Two from the same group always add to a multiple of 4 (8 + 12 = 20, 6 + 10 = 16); one from each group never does (4 + 6 = 10). The same remainder idea pairs 1 to 8 so every pair adds to a multiple of 4: (1, 3), (5, 7), (2, 6), (4, 8) — and (1, 7), (3, 5) also works.
Always, sometimes or never? 'odd + odd is even' is always; 'n² + 1 is even' is sometimes (n = 3 yes, n = 2 no); 'three odd numbers add to an even number' is never.

ex.q: Is 7n + 4 even or odd when n is odd?

topics.rl: Seat-pairing, team-pairing and partner games all hide parity and remainder puzzles.

rv.summary: 2n is always even, 2n + 1 always odd, and n(n + 1) is always even. An odd count of odd numbers gives an odd sum. Remainders on division by 4 decide which pairs add to a multiple of 4, and statements can be always, sometimes or never true.
focus: Find the parity of expressions like 5n + 3
Decide whether a set of odd numbers can reach a given sum
Pair numbers so each pair adds to a multiple of 4
Decide if a statement is always, sometimes or never true
remember: n² has the same parity as n; n(n + 1) is always even
An odd count of odd numbers adds to odd; an even count adds to even
Two evens add to a multiple of 4 only if both are multiples of 4 or both leave remainder 2
'n² + 1 is even' is sometimes true; 'three odd numbers add to even' is never true
traps: Don't decide 'always' from one example
Not every pair of even numbers adds to a multiple of 4 (4 + 6 = 10)
Don't say 3n is always odd: it is odd only when n is odd

topics.h: Diya's number leaves remainder 3 when divided by 5, and Om's leaves 4. What remainder does their sum leave? You don't even need the numbers!
p: If a and b are both multiples of k, then a + b and a − b are multiples of k too: 35 and 21 are multiples of 7, so 56 and 14 are as well.
If a is a multiple of k, then a × b is a multiple of k for every b. But a + b need not be (6 is a multiple of 3; 6 + 4 = 10 is not).
Remainders can be added: if a leaves 3 and b leaves 4 when divided by 5, a + b leaves 3 + 4 = 7, which is 1 five and 2 — remainder 2.
Remainders can be multiplied: a × b leaves the remainder of 3 × 4 = 12, which is 2. For a − b, use 3 − 4 = −1, then add 5 to get 4.

ex.q: a leaves remainder 5 and b leaves remainder 4 when divided by 6. What remainder does a + b leave?

topics.rl: Calendars work with remainders: if today is Monday, 100 days later is a Wednesday because 100 leaves remainder 2 when divided by 7.

rv.summary: If a and b are multiples of k, so are a + b and a − b, and a × b is a multiple of k whenever a is. Remainders can be added, multiplied and subtracted, then reduced to get the remainder of the result.
focus: Decide which combinations of multiples are still multiples
Find the remainder of a sum from the remainders
Find the remainder of a product or difference
Find factors that must divide a number
remember: Multiples of k: a + b and a − b are multiples of k
a multiple of k → a × b is a multiple of k for any b
Remainder of a + b = remainder of (r₁ + r₂); of a × b = remainder of (r₁ × r₂)
For a − b with r₁ < r₂, add the divisor to r₁ − r₂
traps: Don't leave a remainder bigger than the divisor: remainders 5 + 5 on ÷ 6 give 10, which leaves 4
Don't assume adding any number to a multiple keeps it a multiple
If 12 divides a number, its factors (like 4) divide it, not its multiples

topics.h: A riddle: 'Put my pebbles in 2s, 3s, 4s, 5s or 6s and one is always left over; put them in 7s and none are left.' The answer is 301!
p: A number that leaves remainder 1 on division by 2, 3 and 4 is 1 more than a multiple of LCM(2, 3, 4) = 12: 13, 25, 37, ...
Pebble riddle: 1 more than a multiple of LCM(2, 3, 4, 5, 6) = 60, so 61, 121, 181, 241, 301, ... The first one divisible by 7 is 301.
If the remainder is always one less than the divisor (1 for 2, 2 for 3, 3 for 4), then the number + 1 is a common multiple: 11, 23, 35, ...
Nearest multiple of 9: find the remainder with the digit sum. 4567 has digit sum 22 → remainder 4, so 4563 is 4 below and 4572 is 5 above; 4563 is nearest.
Counting multiples in a range: the multiples of 9 from 100 to 200 run from 108 to 198, giving (198 − 108) ÷ 9 + 1 = 11 numbers.

ex.q: Find the smallest number that leaves remainder 1 when divided by 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, and is divisible by 7.

topics.rl: Shopkeepers packing sweets into boxes of different sizes meet these riddles every day!

rv.summary: A number leaving remainder 1 on division by several numbers is 1 more than a multiple of their LCM. If the remainder is always one less than the divisor, the number is 1 less than a common multiple. Digit sums find nearest multiples of 9.
focus: Solve remainder riddles using the LCM
Handle 'remainder one less than the divisor' riddles
Find the nearest multiple of 9 using the digit sum
Count multiples of a number in a range
remember: Remainder 1 on ÷ 2, 3, 4 → 1 more than a multiple of 12
Remainder always one less than the divisor → number + 1 is a common multiple
Digit sum gives the remainder on ÷ 9
Count of multiples = (last − first) ÷ step + 1
traps: Don't leave out an end when counting multiples in a range
Don't choose the nearest multiple without comparing the distances above and below
Check every condition of the riddle, not just some

topics.h: Can you tell whether 7,35,816 is divisible by 8 without dividing at all? Just peek at the last three digits!
p: A number is divisible by 2 if its last digit is even, by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5, and by 10 if it ends in 0.
Divisible by 4: check the number made by the last two digits. This works because 100 is a multiple of 4.
Divisible by 8: check the number made by the last three digits. This works because 1000 = 8 × 125.
A number divisible by 8 is also divisible by 4 and 2, but a number divisible by 4 need not be divisible by 8 (like 12).
The remainder on dividing by 4 is the same as the remainder for the last two digits: 9,147 → 47 → remainder 3.

ex.q: Is 73,512 divisible by 8? Is it divisible by 4?
st: Every multiple of 8 is a multiple of 4
ex.a: Yes, it is divisible by both 8 and 4

topics.rl: Leap years use the rule for 4: the year 2028 is a leap year because 28 is divisible by 4.

rv.summary: Divisibility by 2, 5 and 10 depends on the last digit, by 4 on the last two digits (since 100 is a multiple of 4) and by 8 on the last three digits (since 1000 = 8 × 125).
focus: Test numbers for divisibility by 2, 4, 5, 8 and 10
Fill a missing digit to make a number divisible by 4 or 8
Find the remainder on division by 4 from the last two digits
Explain why the tests work using place value
remember: 2: last digit even; 5: ends in 0 or 5; 10: ends in 0
4: last two digits divisible by 4 (100 = 4 × 25)
8: last three digits divisible by 8 (1000 = 8 × 125)

topics.h: Add the digits of 61,875: 6 + 1 + 8 + 7 + 5 = 27. Because 27 is a multiple of 9, so is 61,875. Magic? No, place value!
p: A number is divisible by 3 if its digit sum is divisible by 3, and divisible by 9 if its digit sum is divisible by 9.
Why it works: 10 = 9 + 1, 100 = 99 + 1, 1000 = 999 + 1. So a number and its digit sum leave the same remainder when divided by 9 (or by 3).
Digital root: keep adding the digits until one digit is left. For 9,875: 29 → 11 → 2, so 9,875 leaves remainder 2 when divided by 9.
Divisible by 6: the number must be divisible by both 2 and 3.
Divisible by 11: starting from the right, subtract and add the digits in turn. If the result is 0 or a multiple of 11, so is the number.

ex.q: Is 61,875 divisible by 9? Is it divisible by 6?
st: 61,875 is odd, so it is not divisible by 2
So it is not divisible by 6

topics.rl: Shopkeepers use digit sums to quickly check bills: if the digital roots do not match, there is a mistake somewhere.

rv.summary: A number is divisible by 3 or 9 if its digit sum is, because 10, 100, 1000, ... are each 1 more than a multiple of 9. Divisibility by 6 needs both 2 and 3, and the alternating sum tests 11.
focus: Test numbers for divisibility by 3, 9, 6 and 11
Find digital roots and remainders on division by 9
Fill a missing digit to make a number divisible by 3
Explain why the digit-sum test works

A number and its digit sum leave the same remainder on ÷ 9
6: divisible by both 2 and 3
11: alternate subtract and add digits from the right; result 0 or a multiple of 11

Don't stop at a 2-digit digit sum; keep adding until one digit is left

topics.h: EF × E = GGG. Three letters, one multiplication, and only one answer. Can you crack the code?
p: In letter puzzles, each letter is a digit. Use place value, last digits, parity and divisibility. GGG = G × 111 = G × 3 × 37, so EF × E = GGG means EF = 37 and E = 3: 37 × 3 = 111.
Place value helps: AB + BA = (10A + B) + (10B + A) = 11(A + B). So AB + BA = 121 means A + B = 11.
Products of consecutive whole numbers: two in a row is always divisible by 2; three in a row by 6; four in a row by 24.

Venn diagrams of multiples: every multiple of 32 is a multiple of 8, and every multiple of 8 is a multiple of 4 — the circles sit inside each other. Multiples of 4 and of 6 overlap in the multiples of 12.

ex.q: Solve EF × E = GGG.
st: EF is a two-digit factor, so EF = 37 (or 74, which fails)

topics.rl: Codes on lockers and puzzles in newspapers use exactly these tricks.

rv.summary: Letter-digit puzzles are cracked with place value, last digits and factors: GGG = G × 3 × 37 and AB + BA = 11(A + B). Products of consecutive numbers have guaranteed factors, and multiples can be shown in nested Venn diagrams.
focus: Solve puzzles like EF × E = GGG and AB + BA
Know what products of 2, 3 and 4 consecutive numbers are divisible by
Decide how sets of multiples sit inside each other
Use place value to find a two-digit number from a clue
remember: AB + BA = 11(A + B)
Product of 2 consecutive numbers: divisible by 2; 3 numbers: by 6; 4 numbers: by 24
Multiples of 32 ⊂ multiples of 8 ⊂ multiples of 4
traps: Letters stand for different digits, so 11 cannot be EF
Don't stop at 12 for four consecutive numbers: it is 24
A multiple of 8 need not be a multiple of 32 (e.g. 40)

topics.h: You know 23 × 17 = 391. What is 24 × 17? Don't start again — just add one more 17!
p: If one factor goes up by 1, the product goes up by the other factor: (a + 1) × b = ab + b. So 24 × 17 = 391 + 17 = 408.
If both factors go up by 1: (a + 1)(b + 1) = ab + a + b + 1.
To keep a product the same, multiply one factor by a number and divide the other by the same number: 12 × 18 = 24 × 9 = 6 × 36 = 216.
Comparing 14 × 26 and 16 × 24: both pairs add to 40. 14 × 26 = (20 − 6)(20 + 6) = 400 − 36 = 364 and 16 × 24 = 400 − 16 = 384. The closer the two numbers, the bigger the product.
topics.rl: Shopkeepers adjust bills quickly this way: if 12 items cost ₹420 at ₹35 each, one more item just adds ₹35.

rv.summary: If one factor goes up by 1, the product goes up by the other factor; if both go up by 1, it goes up by a + b + 1. Multiplying one factor and dividing the other by the same number keeps the product, and closer factors with the same sum give a bigger product.
focus: Find a new product from a known one when a factor changes by 1
Find the change when both factors go up by 1
Keep a product the same by multiplying and dividing
Compare products of pairs with the same sum
remember: (a + 1) × b = ab + b
Multiply one factor by k and divide the other by k: product unchanged
Same sum: the closer the two numbers, the bigger the product (16 × 24 > 14 × 26)
traps: Add the other factor, not 1, when one factor goes up by 1
Don't forget the extra 1 × 1 when both go up by 1
Adding to one factor and subtracting from the other does not keep the product

topics.h: Can you work out 7 × 102 in your head in two seconds? Split 102 into 100 + 2, and it is 700 + 14 = 714!
p: Distributive property: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c. For example, 6 × 47 = 6 × 40 + 6 × 7 = 240 + 42 = 282.
It works with subtraction too: a × (b − c) = a × b − a × c. So 8 × 99 = 800 − 8 = 792.
Area picture: a rectangle a wide and (b + c) long splits into two rectangles with areas ab and ac.
Two brackets: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd. Every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second.
It works for algebra: 3x(2x + 5) = 6x² + 15x.

ex.q: Find 23 × 14 by splitting both numbers.

topics.rl: A shopkeeper selling 6 kurtas at ₹499 each thinks 6 × 500 − 6 × 1 = ₹3000 − ₹6 = ₹2994. Quick and correct!

rv.summary: The distributive property says a × (b + c) = ab + ac and a × (b − c) = ab − ac. It explains mental tricks like 8 × 99 = 800 − 8, and two brackets multiply term by term: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd.

Expand a single bracket with algebra
Expand two brackets and combine like terms
Use area pictures to explain the property

(a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd (4 products)
traps: Multiply every term inside the bracket, not just the first
Don't miss the middle terms when expanding two brackets
Don't lose the signs: (2x + 1)(x − 3) = 2x² − 5x − 3

topics.h: Multiplying (x² + 2x + 3) by (x + 1) looks scary. Put it in a grid and it becomes a simple fill-in-the-boxes game!
p: Grid method: write the terms of one bracket along the top and the other down the side. Fill each box with a product, then add all the boxes and combine like terms.
A trinomial times a binomial gives 3 × 2 = 6 products: (x² + 2x + 3)(x + 1) = x³ + x² + 2x² + 2x + 3x + 3 = x³ + 3x² + 5x + 3.
A beautiful pattern: (a − b)(a + b) = a² − b², (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) = a³ − b³, (a − b)(a³ + a²b + ab² + b³) = a⁴ − b⁴. All the middle terms cancel.

ex.q: Use a grid to expand (2x + 3)(x + 4).

topics.rl: Engineers expand long products when they work out areas and volumes of boxes whose sides change.

rv.summary: In the grid method, each box holds the product of one term from each bracket; add the boxes and combine like terms. A trinomial times a binomial gives 6 products, and (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) = a³ − b³ because the middle terms cancel.

Expand a trinomial times a binomial
Use the (a − b)(...) = aⁿ − bⁿ pattern
Use the pattern for number facts like 9 × 111 = 999

(a − b)(a² + ab + b²) = a³ − b³
traps: Each grid box is a product, not a sum
Don't leave out a like term when collecting (e.g. both x² terms)
Don't confuse (a − b)(a² + ab + b²) with (a − b)³

topics.h: Is (a + b)² the same as a² + b²? Try a = 1 and b = 1: (1 + 1)² = 4 but 1² + 1² = 2. Something is missing!
p: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². In a square of side (a + b), there are two a × b rectangles besides the squares a² and b².
(a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b².
An identity is true for every value of the letters, unlike an equation such as x + 3 = 7, which is true for only one value.

ex.q: Find 51² using an identity.

topics.rl: Builders use (a + b)² when a square courtyard of side a is made b metres longer and b metres wider: the new area is a² + 2ab + b².

rv.summary: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² and (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b². These are identities, true for every value, and they make squares like 103² and 98² easy to find mentally.

topics.t: Difference of squares and quick products
topics.h: 52 × 48 looks hard, but 52 and 48 are 2 more and 2 less than 50. So it is just 50² − 2² = 2496!
p: (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b². The middle terms +ab and −ab cancel out.
Difference of squares the other way: 47² − 43² = (47 + 43)(47 − 43) = 90 × 4 = 360.
Picture: from an a × a square, cut off a b × b corner. The leftover pieces rearrange into a rectangle (a + b) by (a − b).

ex.q: Find 103 × 97 quickly.

topics.rl: Mental-maths champions use (a + b)(a − b) to multiply numbers like 61 × 59 = 3600 − 1 = 3599 in a flash.

rv.summary: (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b² because the middle terms cancel, which gives quick products like 103 × 97 = 9991 and quick differences like 47² − 43² = 90 × 4. Also (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab.

topics.t: Differences of squares and growing patterns
topics.h: Can every number be written as one square minus another? 15 = 8² − 7² and 24 = 7² − 5². But try 6 — you will never manage!
p: Every odd number is a difference of two consecutive squares: 2k + 1 = (k + 1)² − k². So 15 = 8² − 7².

Every multiple of 4 is a difference of squares too: 4k = (k + 1)² − (k − 1)². So 24 = 7² − 5². Numbers like 2, 6, 10, 14 (2 more than a multiple of 4) can never be written this way using whole numbers.
An identity must work for every number — negatives and fractions too. Test (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b² with a = −3, b = 5: both sides give 4.
Growing patterns: a row of y squares made of matchsticks needs 3y + 1 sticks. The border of tiles around a y × y square uses (y + 2)² − y² = 4y + 4 tiles.

ex.q: Write 40 as a difference of two squares.

topics.rl: Tile layers and fence posts follow growing patterns — builders use rules like 4y + 4 to order materials.

rv.summary: Every odd number is a difference of consecutive squares, 2k + 1 = (k + 1)² − k², and every multiple of 4 is 4k = (k + 1)² − (k − 1)²; numbers 2 more than a multiple of 4 never are. Identities hold for negatives and fractions, and they describe growing patterns.

traps: Not every even number fails: multiples of 4 work
Don't subtract fractions before squaring them
Don't forget the corners when counting a border

topics.t: Mind the mistake, mend the mistake
topics.h: Raju wrote (x + 4)² = x² + 16 and got a big red cross. What went wrong? Let's become algebra doctors and fix the mistakes!
p: (a + b)² is NOT a² + b². The middle term 2ab is missing: (x + 4)² = x² + 8x + 16.
(a − b)² is NOT a² − b²: (x − 5)² = x² − 10x + 25.
A minus sign before a bracket changes every sign inside: 5 − (x − 2) = 5 − x + 2 = 7 − x.
Multiply every term inside: 3(a + 4) = 3a + 12, not 3a + 4. And (2y)² = 4y², not 2y².
Only like terms combine: 4x + 3y stays as it is — it is not 7xy. A quick test with numbers catches most mistakes.

ex.q: Raju says (a + b)² = a² + b². Test with a = 2, b = 3.
st: So the correct rule is a² + 2ab + b²
ex.a: Raju is wrong: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²

topics.rl: Checking answers by putting in simple numbers is what good engineers and accountants do every day.

rv.summary: Common algebra slips: (a + b)² is not a² + b², (a − b)² is not a² − b², a minus before a bracket changes every sign inside, every term in a bracket must be multiplied, and only like terms combine. A quick number test catches most mistakes.

topics.h: Two friends find the area of the same L-shaped room. One adds, the other subtracts. Different methods — but the answers must match!
p: A shaded area can be found by adding pieces, or by subtracting from a bigger shape. The answers are equal, so the two expressions are equivalent.
L-shape from a big square of side a with a b × b corner cut out: area a² − b². Cut it into two rectangles instead: (a + b)(a − b). So a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b).
Path outside a plot: (outer rectangle) − (plot). A plot l by w with a path of width p all round has path area (l + 2p)(w + 2p) − lw.
For a square plot of side a with a path of width p outside: (a + 2p)² − a² = 4ap + 4p².
Two expressions are equivalent if they simplify to the same thing, like x(x + 5) + 3x and x² + 8x.

ex.q: A garden 20 m by 12 m has a 2 m wide path all round outside it. Find the path's area.

topics.rl: Builders calculate paths around parks and borders around swimming pools exactly this way.

rv.summary: An area can be found by adding pieces or by subtracting from a bigger shape, and both expressions are equal. This shows a² − b² = (a + b)(a − b), and path areas are outer area minus inner area.

topics.h: Circle any 2 × 2 block of dates on a calendar. Multiply across the diagonals and subtract. You will ALWAYS get 7. Why?
p: Calendar trick: a 2 × 2 block has dates a, a + 1 (top) and a + 7, a + 8 (below). (a + 1)(a + 7) − a(a + 8) = a² + 8a + 7 − a² − 8a = 7. Always 7!
Middle-square trick: for three consecutive numbers, the middle one squared is 1 more than the product of the other two: n² − (n − 1)(n + 1) = 1. So 24² − 23 × 25 = 1.
Proving statements: (k + 1)(k + 2) − (k + 3) = k² + 2k − 1 = (k + 1)² − 2. So it is always 2 less than a perfect square.
Remainders on division by 7: if a leaves 3 and b leaves 5, then a + b leaves 3 + 5 = 8 → 1, and a × b leaves 3 × 5 = 15 → 1.

ex.q: Check the calendar trick on the block 12, 13 / 19, 20.
st: Algebra shows it is 7 for every block

topics.rl: Magicians use such provable tricks; mathematicians enjoy showing exactly why they never fail.

rv.summary: Algebra proves number tricks: in any 2 × 2 calendar block the diagonal products differ by 7, the middle of three consecutive numbers squared is 1 more than the product of the other two, and remainders can be added or multiplied.

traps: One example is not a proof; use algebra
The two diagonal products are not equal
Don't leave a remainder bigger than the divisor; reduce it

topics.h: Stretch a selfie by adding 4 cm to both its width and height, and your face looks squashed. Multiply both by 2, and it looks perfect. Why?
p: Two pictures look alike when the width and height are both multiplied by the same number. A 4 cm × 6 cm photo enlarged to 8 cm × 12 cm (both × 2) keeps its shape.
Adding the same amount to both sides distorts the picture: 4 × 6 becomes 8 × 10 when 4 is added, and the ratio changes from 2 : 3 to 4 : 5.
Quantities are proportional when they change by the same multiplying factor.
Ages show this well: Ravi is 5 and his father is 30 (1 : 6). After 5 years they are 10 and 35, which is 2 : 7 — not 1 : 6. Adding the same number of years changes the ratio.

ex.q: A 3 cm × 5 cm photo is enlarged without distortion so its width is 9 cm. What is its height?

topics.rl: Phone screens and TV screens are sold in fixed shapes such as 16 : 9 so pictures never look stretched.

Scale by multiplying, not by adding the extra people

topics.h: Nimbu pani tastes perfect with 1 spoon of sugar for every 2 glasses of water. For 6 glasses you need 3 spoons. That is a ratio at work!
p: A ratio a : b compares two quantities of the same kind by division. 12 boys and 18 girls give 12 : 18 = 2 : 3.
Use the same unit before writing a ratio: 50 cm : 2 m = 50 cm : 200 cm = 1 : 4.
Equivalent ratios come from multiplying or dividing both terms by the same non-zero number: 2 : 3 = 4 : 6 = 10 : 15.
Order matters: 2 : 3 is not the same as 3 : 2.
Part-to-whole: if boys : girls = 2 : 3, then boys are 2 out of every 5 children, that is 2/5 of the class.

ex.q: Write 45 minutes : 2 hours in simplest form.
st: Change to the same unit: 2 hours = 120 minutes

topics.rl: Recipes, mixing cement and sand, and the 3 : 2 shape of the Indian flag all use ratios.

topics.h: On a map, Delhi to Agra is just 4 cm, but the real road is about 200 km long. Maps work because distances are in proportion!
p: Four numbers are in proportion when a : b = c : d. We write a : b :: c : d.
Cross-multiplication test: a : b :: c : d exactly when a × d = b × c. (Product of extremes = product of means.)
To find a missing term: 3 : 4 :: 12 : x means 3x = 4 × 12 = 48, so x = 16.
Proportion uses multiplication, not addition. Going from 3 to 12 is ×4, so 4 becomes 16 (not 4 + 9 = 13).
A map scale of 1 : 50,000 means 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm = 500 m on the ground.

ex.q: Meena makes 12 laddoos with 2 cups of besan. How much besan does she need for 30 laddoos?

topics.rl: Shopkeepers, cooks, map readers and photo editors all scale things up and down in proportion.

rv.summary: Four numbers are in proportion, a : b :: c : d, when the ratios are equal, which happens exactly when a × d = b × c. Missing terms are found by cross-multiplying, and map scales are proportions.

topics.t: Unitary method and sharing in a ratio
topics.h: Is a ₹60 pack of 500 g biscuits a better deal than a ₹84 pack of 750 g? Find the price of the same amount and you will know!
p: Unitary method: first find the value of ONE unit, then multiply for as many units as you need.
5 kg of apples cost ₹600, so 1 kg costs ₹120 and 8 kg cost ₹960.
To compare deals, find the price per gram, per 100 g or per kg. The lower unit price is the better buy.
To divide an amount in the ratio a : b, add the parts (a + b), find one part, then multiply.
₹900 in the ratio 4 : 5: 9 parts, 1 part = ₹100, so the shares are ₹400 and ₹500.

ex.q: 3 pens cost ₹45. What do 7 pens cost?

topics.rl: Comparing prices at a market, splitting a taxi fare, or sharing prize money in a ratio all use the unitary method.

rv.summary: The unitary method first finds the value of one unit, then multiplies. Unit prices show the better buy, and to share in a ratio a : b you add the parts, find one part, then multiply.

Compare deals using unit prices

Lower unit price = better buy

topics.t: Mixtures and the rule of three
topics.h: Indian mathematicians had a name for the method you use to scale recipes: trairāśika, the rule of three. It's over 1500 years old!
p: Compare strengths of mixtures by the fraction of the strong part. Coffee 1 : 3 (decoction : milk) has 1/4 decoction; 2 : 5 has 2/7 ≈ 0.29. So 2 : 5 is stronger.
Rule of three: if a gives b, then c gives d = b × c ÷ a. In Sanskrit: pramāṇa (a), phala (b), icchā (c) and icchāphala (d, the answer).
Change to the same units before setting up the proportion: if 500 g cost ₹30, then 2 kg = 2000 g cost 30 × 2000 ÷ 500 = ₹120.
The rule of three works only when the quantities grow together. If 4 workers take 6 days, 8 workers do NOT take 12 days — more workers take fewer days (3 days). These are inversely related.

ex.q: 5 kg of rice costs ₹225. Use the rule of three to find the cost of 8 kg.
st: pramāṇa a = 5 kg, phala b = ₹225, icchā c = 8 kg

topics.rl: Chefs, pharmacists and paint mixers all use the rule of three every working day.

rv.summary: Compare mixtures by the fraction of the strong part. The rule of three says if a gives b, then c gives b × c ÷ a, with Sanskrit names pramāṇa, phala, icchā and icchāphala. It works only when quantities grow together.

In a mixture, find the amount of each part first. 20 L of milk and water in the ratio 3 : 1 has 15 L milk and 5 L water.

topics.t: Converting units: length, area and volume

p: Length units are linked by fixed ratios: 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 foot = 30.48 cm, 1 inch = 2.54 cm.
Area ratios are the squares of length ratios: 1 m² = 100 × 100 = 10,000 cm², and 1 m² ≈ 10.76 sq ft.
Land is measured in hectares and acres: 1 hectare = 10,000 m², and 1 acre ≈ 4047 m² (about 0.4 hectare).

p: Percentage change = (change ÷ original value) × 100.
Always divide by the ORIGINAL (starting) value, not the new value.
Increase by r%: new value = original × (100 + r)/100. So ₹200 up by 10% = ₹200 × 1.1 = ₹220.
Decrease by r%: new value = original × (100 − r)/100. So ₹500 down by 20% = ₹500 × 0.8 = ₹400.
Up 10% then down 10% does NOT bring you back: 100 → 110 → 99.

topics.h: A shopkeeper marks a kurta at ₹800, gives a 20% discount, and still makes a profit. How? It cost him only ₹500!
p: Cost price (CP) is what the seller paid. Selling price (SP) is what the buyer pays.
If SP > CP there is a profit: Profit = SP − CP. If CP > SP there is a loss: Loss = CP − SP.
Profit % and loss % are always worked out on the cost price: Profit % = Profit/CP × 100.
Marked price (MP) is the price on the tag. Discount = MP − SP, and discount % is worked out on the marked price.
After a discount of r%, SP = MP × (100 − r)/100.

p: Percentages can be more than 100: 150% of 80 = 1.5 × 80 = 120. If a price becomes 2.5 times, the new price is 250% of the old (a 150% increase).
GST is added as a percentage of the price: ₹800 + 18% GST = 800 × 1.18 = ₹944.
Marking up by r% and then giving r% off ends below the start: 100 → 120 → 96 for r = 20. That is a 4% loss.
Area changes multiply: if each side of a square grows by 10%, the area becomes 1.1 × 1.1 = 1.21 times — a 21% increase, not 20%.
If length goes up 20% and breadth goes down 20%, the area becomes 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96 times — a 4% decrease.

topics.h: Put ₹1000 in a bank at 10% and leave it. With compound interest it is ₹1210 after 2 years — interest earns interest!
p: Simple interest is paid only on the original amount p: amount after t years = p(1 + rt). ₹5000 at 8% for 3 years: 5000 × 1.24 = ₹6200.
Compound interest adds each year's interest to the amount, so next year's interest is bigger: amount = p(1 + r)ᵗ. ₹5000 at 8% for 3 years: 5000 × 1.08³ ≈ ₹6298.56.
Depreciation (losing value) works by repeated multiplication too: a scooter worth ₹60,000 losing 10% a year is worth 60,000 × 0.9 × 0.9 = ₹48,600 after 2 years.
Populations and prices (inflation) grow the same way: 20,000 people growing 5% a year become 20,000 × 1.05² = 22,050 after 2 years.
Percentage share: a family spending ₹12,000 of ₹40,000 on food spends 30% on food.
